title: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But there is also reason to believe, that those species which are very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges”. Scope: plants (British flora), extended to species generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.87

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global occurrences and phylogenies make both variables available across many taxa. The association and major confounds can be assessed with standard comparative models.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate each species' range size to its nearest-neighbor genetic or phylogenetic distance, controlling clade, latitude and observation effort. Smaller ranges among closest relatives support the claim; no or opposite association refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Occurrence-derived ranges are sensitive to sampling.

Recent species may have small ranges for reasons unrelated to variety status.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range surfaces and phylogenies make this regression a standard macroecological test for birds, mammals, and many plants. Adequacy is that of well-mapped groups rather than species generally, matching a claim that started from the British flora and was generalized. Description bias and age-range correlations are serious, and they are quantifiable, so the result can be informative without being fully clean.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress geographic range size on distance to the nearest congener, phylogenetically or morphologically defined. Smaller ranges for the closest species would support the pattern; no relationship, or larger ranges for the closest species, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Recently described close species are often known from few localities, which shrinks apparent range.

Young species may have small ranges because they are young, which is related to the claim but not identical to a variety-like restriction.

Occurrence-based ranges under-represent poorly sampled regions and narrow endemics differently.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among seed plant species, those that split most recently from their closest sampled relative (shortest terminal branch on a dated molecular phylogeny) have smaller native ranges than their congeners with longer terminal branches.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Tip labels and terminal branch lengths were read from GBMB.tre (79,874 tips) and matched exactly to WCVP accepted non-hybrid species binomials; range size was the number of TDWG level-3 regions with a non-doubtful, native, non-extinct record (63,306 tips matched with a range). Genera with >= 5 matched species covering >= 50% of the genus's accepted species qualified (783 genera, 16,223 species; 716 with variation in both variables). Within each genus the Spearman correlation between terminal branch length and range size was computed, and the correlations were combined by Fisher z weighted by n - 3 with a two-sided z test; species of genera with a native British species were analysed the same way as a descriptive secondary.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: tips of the GBMB tree of Smith & Brown 2018 (dated seed plant phylogeny built from GenBank sequences only) are matched exactly (binomial, underscores to spaces) to WCVP accepted non-hybrid species. Nearest-relative distance d = terminal branch length (Myr). Range size r = number of TDWG level-3 regions with a non-doubtful native, non-extinct WCVP record (species with r = 0 dropped). Genera qualify if >= 5 matched species and matched species >= 50% of the genus's WCVP accepted species. Within each qualifying genus, Spearman rho_g between d and r; the summary is the mean of Fisher-z(rho_g) weighted by (n_g - 3), back-transformed, with a two-sided combined z test. SUPPORTS if the weighted mean rho >= 0.10, combined p < 0.01 and rho_g > 0 in more than half of qualifying genera with at least one non-tied variable.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the weighted mean rho <= 0. Any other outcome (0 < rho < 0.10, or not significant, or positive in at most half of genera) is MIXED. Fewer than 30 qualifying genera: inconclusive (underpowered). Tree or WCVP unobtainable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). Descriptive secondary statistics: the same weighted rho restricted to species native to Great Britain (GRB) genera with >= 3 matched species, and the pooled Spearman rho without genus stratification.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: weighted mean within-genus Spearman rho between terminal branch length (Myr) and number of native TDWG level-3 regions

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: combined two-sided p=0.00232; species in qualifying genera=16223

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties' is read as a short phylogenetic distance to the nearest relative, measured as the terminal branch length on a dated tree (half the patristic distance to the sister lineage). 'Much restricted ranges' is read as the number of botanical-country (TDWG level-3) units in which the species is native, a coarse range measure. Stratifying by genus controls clade differences in range size and rate; the sampling threshold limits inflation of terminal branches by unsampled relatives. Darwin's scope began with the British flora and extended to species generally; the global seed plant test is the general reading and the British subset is descriptive. Molecular divergence is a modern stand-in for Darwin's morphological closeness.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Smith & Brown 2018, Constructing a broadly inclusive seed plant phylogeny (GBMB: GenBank-only dated tree with Magallón et al. 2015 backbone), release v0.1

World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The association runs in Darwin's direction and is statistically detectable (weighted within-genus rho = 0.026, p = 0.002; 51% of genera positive; pooled rho without stratification 0.063; genera with British natives rho = 0.053), but it is far below the pre-registered support threshold of 0.10 and the median number of native regions is the same (2) in the quarter of species with the shortest and the quarter with the longest terminal branches within their genus. Hence MIXED: close relatedness explains almost none of the variation in range size.

Terminal branch length measures time since splitting from the closest sampled relative, not morphological closeness or 'variety-like' status, which is what Darwin observed; unsampled relatives lengthen terminal branches despite the 50% sampling threshold.

Range size is counted in TDWG level-3 botanical countries, a coarse unit: most species occupy 1-3 units, producing many ties that weaken rank correlations and cannot capture restriction within a country (Darwin's British examples).

GBMB dates rely on a backbone and secondary calibrations; terminal branches in poorly resolved genera are imprecise.

Name matching is exact on binomials; tree names that are synonyms in WCVP were dropped (about 21% of tips were unmatched or had no native range).
